---
title: "Performance"
description: >
  Compare Panache's formatting, linting, and language-server performance with
  other Markdown and Quarto tools on individual documents, whole repositories,
  and editor sessions.
engine: knitr
---

## Overview

These benchmarks compare Panache's formatting, linting, and language-server
performance with other Markdown and Quarto tools. They measure individual
documents, whole repositories, and editor sessions. Tools differ in supported
syntax, formatting policy, lint coverage, and editor features, so timings should
be read alongside the work each tool performs.

The formatting and linting comparisons cover Markdown and Quarto documents; R
Markdown is outside the current corpus. The language-server comparisons use
separate Markdown and Quarto workloads to measure startup, responses to editor
requests, performance after edits, and memory use.

The timing charts use a logarithmic scale in milliseconds; lower is faster.
Formatting and linting charts show mean times, with colors identifying documents
or repositories. Language-server charts show medians, with colors identifying
measurements. Hover over a point for details. Tools are ordered from fastest to
slowest on average in the formatting and linting charts.

```{bash}
#| label: run-benchmarks
#| echo: false
#| output: false
#| eval: false

cd ../..
bash benches/compare_all.sh --json --out docs/guide/performance_data.json
```

```{ojs}
//| label: load-data
//| echo: false

data = FileAttachment("performance_data.json").json();
```

```{ojs}
//| label: prepare-records
//| echo: false

timeTicks = (times) => {
    const [min, max] = d3.extent(times);
    return d3
        .range(Math.floor(Math.log10(min)), Math.ceil(Math.log10(max)) + 1)
        .flatMap((exponent) => [1, 2, 5].map((value) => value * 10 ** exponent))
        .filter((value) => value >= min && value <= max);
};

documentMeta = new Map(data.documents.map((d) => [d.id, d]));

records = data.results.map((r) => ({
    formatter: r.formatter,
    document: r.document,
    documentName: documentMeta.get(r.document)?.name ?? r.document,
    mean_ms: r.mean_ms,
    runs: r.runs,
}));

formatters = Array.from(
    d3.rollup(
        records,
        (v) => d3.mean(v, (d) => d.mean_ms),
        (d) => d.formatter,
    ),
)
    .sort(([, a], [, b]) => a - b)
    .map(([k]) => k);

documentIds = data.documents.map((d) => d.id);
```

```{ojs}
//| label: render-environment
//| echo: false

html`<div class="callout-note">
  <div class="callout-header" style="font-weight: 600">Test Environment</div>
  <ul style="margin: 0">
    <li>Generated: ${new Date(data.meta.generated_at).toUTCString()}</li>
    <li>Host: ${data.meta.host.cpu} (${data.meta.host.os}/${data.meta.host.arch})</li>
    <li>Minimum runs: ${data.meta.min_runs}</li>
    <li>panache ${data.meta.tools.panache.version}, prettier ${data.meta.tools.prettier?.version ?? "n/a"}, pandoc ${data.meta.tools.pandoc?.version ?? "n/a"}, rumdl ${data.meta.tools.rumdl?.version ?? "n/a"}, mdformat ${data.meta.tools.mdformat?.version ?? "n/a"}, yamark ${data.meta.tools.yamark?.version ?? "n/a"}, mado ${data.meta.tools.mado?.version ?? "n/a"}, markdownlint ${data.meta.tools.markdownlint?.version ?? "n/a"}, markdownlint-cli2 ${data.meta.tools["markdownlint-cli2"]?.version ?? "n/a"}</li>
  </ul>
</div>`;
```

## Formatting

### Single-Document

We compare `panache format` with Prettier, Pandoc, rumdl, mdformat, and Yamark
on individual documents (@fig-plot-results). Each command formats one document
in a fresh process, so the timings include startup overhead.

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-plot-results
//| echo: false
//| fig-cap: "Mean formatting time per document. Each dot represents one
//|   document, identified by color."

Plot.plot({
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginRight: 20,
    marginBottom: 40,
    marginTop: 20,
    height: 360,
    x: { label: null, domain: formatters },
    y: {
        type: "log",
        tickFormat: d3.format(",~g"),
        ticks: timeTicks(records.map((d) => d.mean_ms)),
        label: "Mean time (ms, log scale; lower is faster)",
        grid: true,
    },
    color: {
        legend: true,
        domain: documentIds,
        tickFormat: (id) => documentMeta.get(id)?.name ?? id,
        scheme: "tableau10",
    },
    marks: [
        Plot.dot(records, {
            x: "formatter",
            y: "mean_ms",
            fill: "document",
            r: 6,
            fillOpacity: 0.85,
            stroke: "white",
            strokeWidth: 1,
            channels: {
                document: "documentName",
                "time (ms)": (d) => d.mean_ms.toFixed(1),
            },
            tip: true,
        }),
    ],
});
```

```{ojs}
//| label: prepare-repo-suite-helper
//| echo: false

prepareRepoSuiteRows = (data, toolLabels) => {
    const repoMeta = new Map(data.repos.map((r) => [r.id, r]));

    return data.results
        .filter((r) => !r.failed && r.mean_ms > 0)
        .map((r) => {
            const repo = repoMeta.get(r.repo);
            const repoLabel = repo?.name ?? r.repo;
            const toolLabel = toolLabels[r.tool] ?? r.tool;
            return {
                ...r,
                repoLabel,
                toolLabel,
                fileCount: repo?.file_count ?? null,
                totalBytes: repo?.total_bytes ?? null,
            };
        });
};
```

In the recorded runs, Yamark has the shortest mean time on every document,
followed by Panache. The tools perform different work, including different
handling of math; the [methodology](#methodology) describes those differences.

### Repository-Wide

These comparisons run each formatter once per repository, processing its tracked
Markdown or Quarto files together. They capture the cost of formatting many
files in a single invocation.

```{bash}

#| echo: false
#| output: false

bash benches/compare_repo_suite.sh --mode format --track markdown --out docs/guide/performance_repo_markdown_format_data.json
```

## Linting

We compare `panache lint`, `rumdl check`, `mado check`, `markdownlint`, and
`markdownlint-cli2`. Each linter checks for a different set of problems, so
these timings compare the tools' respective checks.

### Single-Document

```{bash}
#| label: run-lint-single-benchmark
#| echo: false
#| output: false
#| eval: false

cd ../..
bash benches/compare_lint_single.sh --out docs/guide/performance_lint_single_data.json
```

```{ojs}
//| label: load-lint-single-data
//| echo: false

lintSingleData = FileAttachment("performance_lint_single_data.json").json();
```

```{ojs}
//| label: prepare-lint-single-records
//| echo: false

lintDocumentMeta = new Map(lintSingleData.documents.map((d) => [d.id, d]));
lintSingleRecords = lintSingleData.results.map((r) => ({
    tool: r.tool,
    document: r.document,
    documentName: lintDocumentMeta.get(r.document)?.name ?? r.document,
    mean_ms: r.mean_ms,
    runs: r.runs,
}));
lintTools = Array.from(
    d3.rollup(
        lintSingleRecords,
        (v) => d3.mean(v, (d) => d.mean_ms),
        (d) => d.tool,
    ),
)
    .sort(([, a], [, b]) => a - b)
    .map(([k]) => k);
lintDocumentIds = lintSingleData.documents.map((d) => d.id);
```

The individual-file comparison uses the same documents as the formatting
benchmark (@fig-lint-single-results). Each invocation starts a fresh process.

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-lint-single-results
//| echo: false
//| fig-cap: "Mean linting time per document. Each dot represents one
//|   document, identified by color."

Plot.plot({
    marginLeft: 60,
    marginRight: 20,
    marginBottom: 40,
    marginTop: 20,
    height: 300,
    x: { label: null, domain: lintTools },
    y: {
        type: "log",
        tickFormat: d3.format(",~g"),
        ticks: timeTicks(lintSingleRecords.map((d) => d.mean_ms)),
        label: "Mean time (ms, log scale; lower is faster)",
        grid: true,
    },
    color: {
        legend: true,
        domain: lintDocumentIds,
        tickFormat: (id) => lintDocumentMeta.get(id)?.name ?? id,
        scheme: "tableau10",
    },
    marks: [
        Plot.dot(lintSingleRecords, {
            x: "tool",
            y: "mean_ms",
            fill: "document",
            r: 6,
            fillOpacity: 0.85,
            stroke: "white",
            strokeWidth: 1,
            channels: {
                document: "documentName",
                "time (ms)": (d) => d.mean_ms.toFixed(1),
            },
            tip: true,
        }),
    ],
});
```

Mado has the shortest mean time on five of the six documents in these runs;
Panache has the shortest time on the remaining document. Both take longer on the
Pandoc manual than on the other inputs.

## Markdown Language Server

We compare Panache with [Marksman](https://github.com/artempyanykh/marksman) by
opening the five largest tracked Markdown files in a pinned revision of the Rust
Book. Each session requests diagnostics and navigation features, then performs
1,000 reference-label edits. A definition request follows each edit to check
that the server has observed the change.

The benchmark measures startup, responses to editor requests, performance after
edits, and memory use across three fresh sessions per server. Marksman indexes
the Markdown workspace eagerly, while Panache analyzes open documents and
discovers project relationships lazily. The results reflect those different
strategies.

```{ojs}
//| label: load-lsp-memory
//| echo: false

lspMemory = FileAttachment("performance_lsp_memory_data.json").json();
```

```{ojs}
//| label: prepare-lsp-memory
//| echo: false

lspMemoryMilestones = [
    { key: "baseline", label: "Baseline" },
    { key: "settled", label: "Files open" },
    { key: "edited", label: "After edits" },
    { key: "peak", label: "Peak" },
];

lspMemoryRows = lspMemory.servers.flatMap((server) =>
    lspMemoryMilestones.map((milestone) => ({
        server: server.label,
        milestone: milestone.label,
        rss: server.aggregate.milestones[milestone.key].rss_mb,
        pss: server.aggregate.milestones[milestone.key].pss_mb,
    })),
);

lspServers = lspMemory.servers.map((server) => server.label);
```

```{ojs}
//| label: render-lsp-memory-environment
//| echo: false

html`<div class="callout-note">
  <div class="callout-header" style="font-weight: 600">Test Environment</div>
  <ul style="margin: 0">
    <li>Generated: ${new Date(lspMemory.meta.generated_at).toUTCString()}</li>
    <li>Host: ${lspMemory.meta.host.cpu} (${lspMemory.meta.host.os}/${lspMemory.meta.host.arch}, ${lspMemory.meta.host.memory_gb} GiB RAM)</li>
    <li>Corpus: ${lspMemory.corpus.name} at ${lspMemory.corpus.revision.slice(0, 12)}; ${lspMemory.session.file_count} open files (${(lspMemory.session.opened_bytes / 1024).toFixed(1)} KiB)</li>
    <li>Workload: ${lspMemory.meta.edit_count.toLocaleString()} edits; ${lspMemory.meta.runs} fresh processes per server</li>
    <li>Warm requests: ${lspMemory.meta.latency_warmups} warmup rounds and ${lspMemory.meta.latency_runs} measured rounds per target in each process</li>
    <li>${lspMemory.servers.map((server) => `${server.label}: ${server.version.replace(/^panache /, "")}`).join(", ")}</li>
  </ul>
</div>`;
```

### Startup and Edit Runtime

@fig-lsp-runtime measures four stages:

- **Initialize** measures the time from process launch to the server's response
  to the editor's initialization request.
- **Workspace ready** measures the time from process launch until background
  work settles after initialization.
- **Open files ready** measures the time from opening the documents until
  diagnostics arrive, initial navigation requests finish, and background work
  settles.
- **Edit workload** measures the time to complete all reference-label edits and
  their definition requests.

Readiness estimates exclude the deliberate wait used to confirm that background
work has settled. The [methodology](#markdown-sessions) explains how the runner
identifies these quiet periods.

```{ojs}
//| label: prepare-lsp-runtime
//| echo: false

lspRuntimeMetrics = [
    { key: "init_seconds", label: "Initialize" },
    { key: "workspace_ready_seconds", label: "Workspace ready" },
    { key: "documents_ready_seconds", label: "Open files ready" },
    { key: "edit_work_seconds", label: "Edit workload" },
];

lspRuntimeRows = lspRuntimeMetrics.flatMap((metric) =>
    lspMemory.servers.map((server) => ({
        server: server.label,
        row: metric.label,
        median: server.aggregate.timings[metric.key] * 1000,
        min: d3.min(server.runs, (run) => run[metric.key]) * 1000,
        max: d3.max(server.runs, (run) => run[metric.key]) * 1000,
    })),
);

lspRuntimeDomain = d3
    .scaleLog()
    .domain(d3.extent(lspRuntimeRows, (d) => d.median))
    .nice()
    .domain();
```

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-lsp-runtime
//| echo: false
//| fig-cap: "Language-server startup and edit runtime on a logarithmic scale.
//|   Tools appear on the x-axis; colors identify runtime metrics. Dots show
//|   medians in milliseconds; tooltips include the minimum and maximum across
//|   fresh processes. Lower is faster."

Plot.plot({
    width,
    marginLeft: 70,
    marginRight: 25,
    marginBottom: 50,
    height: 360,
    x: { label: null, domain: lspServers },
    y: {
        type: "log",
        tickFormat: d3.format(",~g"),
        ticks: timeTicks(lspRuntimeDomain),
        domain: lspRuntimeDomain,
        label: "Elapsed time (ms, log scale)",
        grid: true,
    },
    color: {
        legend: true,
        domain: lspRuntimeMetrics.map((d) => d.label),
        scheme: "tableau10",
    },
    marks: [
        Plot.dot(lspRuntimeRows, {
            x: "server",
            y: "median",
            fill: "row",
            r: 5,
            title: (d) =>
                `${d.row} — ${d.server}\nMedian: ${d.median.toFixed(2)} ms\nRange: ${d.min.toFixed(2)}–${d.max.toFixed(2)} ms`,
            tip: true,
        }),
    ],
});
```

### Request Latency

After startup, we time requests for document symbols, hover information,
definitions, references, and renaming. @fig-lsp-latency shows median response
times, with the 95th percentile (p95) in tooltips. **Edit to definition**
includes both the change notification and the following definition response,
capturing the work needed to observe an edited document.

Tooltips also show result counts and sizes, which can differ between servers.
Points marked "empty" returned no items in any measured request; their timings
measure the overhead of responding without a result.

```{ojs}
//| label: prepare-lsp-latency
//| echo: false

lspLatencyRows = lspMemory.servers[0].aggregate.request_latencies.flatMap(
    (request) =>
        lspMemory.servers.map((server) => {
            const result = server.aggregate.request_latencies.find(
                (r) => r.key === request.key,
            );
            return {
                ...result,
                server: server.label,
                row: request.label,
            };
        }),
);

lspLatencyTip = (d) =>
    `${d.row} — ${d.server}\nMedian: ${d.median_ms.toFixed(3)} ms\np95: ${d.p95_ms.toFixed(3)} ms\nSamples: ${d.samples}; empty: ${d.empty_results}\nReturned items: ${d.result_count_min}–${d.result_count_max}\nFiles involved: ${d.result_files_min == null ? "n/a" : `${d.result_files_min}–${d.result_files_max}`}\nMedian result size: ${d.payload_bytes_median} bytes`;

lspLatencyExtent = d3.extent(lspLatencyRows, (d) => d.median_ms);

lspLatencyDomain = d3.scaleLog().domain(lspLatencyExtent).nice().domain();
```

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-lsp-latency
//| echo: false
//| fig-cap: "Language-server request latency on a logarithmic scale. Tools
//|   appear on the x-axis; colors identify requests. Dots show medians in
//|   milliseconds; tooltips include p95. Lower is faster."

Plot.plot({
    width,
    marginLeft: 70,
    marginRight: 25,
    marginBottom: 50,
    height: 380,
    x: { label: null, domain: lspServers },
    y: {
        type: "log",
        tickFormat: d3.format(",~g"),
        ticks: timeTicks(lspLatencyDomain),
        domain: lspLatencyDomain,
        label: "Request latency (ms, log scale)",
        grid: true,
    },
    color: {
        legend: true,
        domain: lspMemory.servers[0].aggregate.request_latencies.map(
            (d) => d.label,
        ),
        scheme: "tableau10",
    },
    marks: [
        Plot.dot(lspLatencyRows, {
            x: "server",
            y: "median_ms",
            fill: "row",
            r: 5,
            title: lspLatencyTip,
            tip: true,
        }),
        Plot.text(
            lspLatencyRows.filter((d) => d.empty_results === d.samples),
            {
                x: "server",
                y: "median_ms",
                text: () => "empty",
                fill: "row",
                textAnchor: "start",
                dx: 7,
                dy: -10,
            },
        ),
    ],
});
```

Warm symbol, definition, and reference requests have median response times below
one millisecond for both servers in these runs. Requests after edits take
longer, especially for Marksman. Panache's hover and rename requests return
empty results on this target, so their timings do not establish comparable
feature performance.

### Memory

@fig-lsp-memory shows median memory use across three fresh sessions, including
child processes. **RSS** counts resident memory, including shared pages in each
process. Tooltips also show **PSS**, which divides shared pages among the
processes using them to estimate their share of physical memory.

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-lsp-memory
//| echo: false
//| fig-cap: "Median whole-process-tree RSS during the language-server workload.
//|   Each milestone is measured after quiescence, except peak, which is the
//|   largest 150 ms sample from the complete session."

Plot.plot({
    marginLeft: 55,
    marginRight: 20,
    marginBottom: 40,
    marginTop: 25,
    height: 320,
    x: { label: null },
    y: { label: "Median process-tree RSS (MB)", grid: true },
    fx: { label: null, domain: lspMemoryMilestones.map((d) => d.label) },
    color: { legend: true, domain: lspServers, scheme: "tableau10" },
    marks: [
        Plot.barY(lspMemoryRows, {
            fx: "milestone",
            x: "server",
            y: "rss",
            fill: "server",
            channels: { "PSS (MB)": "pss" },
            tip: true,
        }),
        Plot.text(lspMemoryRows, {
            fx: "milestone",
            x: "server",
            y: "rss",
            text: (d) => d.rss.toFixed(1),
            dy: -7,
        }),
    ],
});
```

Panache uses less resident memory at every measured stage in these runs. This
workload opens only five files from the project, so the difference should be
read alongside the servers' approaches to workspace indexing.

## Quarto Language Server

We compare Panache with [`q2 lsp`](https://github.com/quarto-dev/q2), the
experimental Rust Quarto language server, using three authoring guides from a
pinned q2 revision: computations, Markdown basics, and title blocks. The files
live in a standalone project; neither server builds a whole-project index in
this workload.

Each session opens the three files, requests their outlines, and performs 100
heading edits in the computations guide. This comparison covers diagnostics and
document symbols; q2 does not implement the navigation features used in the
Markdown comparison.

Panache returns diagnostics on request, while q2 sends them after processing an
open or change notification. The timings include those different delivery paths
and each server's own checks.

```{ojs}
//| label: load-lsp-quarto
//| echo: false

quartoLsp = FileAttachment("performance_lsp_quarto_data.json").json();

quartoLspLatencies = quartoLsp.servers.flatMap((server) =>
    server.aggregate.request_latencies.map((metric) => ({
        server: server.label,
        metric: metric.label,
        median: metric.median_ms,
        p95: metric.p95_ms,
        samples: metric.samples,
        results: metric.result_count_median,
    })),
);
```

```{ojs}
//| label: render-lsp-quarto-environment
//| echo: false

html`<div class="callout-note">
  <div class="callout-header" style="font-weight: 600">Test Environment</div>
  <ul style="margin: 0">
    <li>Generated: ${new Date(quartoLsp.meta.generated_at).toUTCString()}</li>
    <li>Host: ${quartoLsp.meta.host.cpu} (${quartoLsp.meta.host.os}/${quartoLsp.meta.host.arch}, ${quartoLsp.meta.host.memory_gb} GiB RAM)</li>
    <li>Corpus: ${quartoLsp.corpus.revision.slice(0, 12)}; ${quartoLsp.session.file_count} files (${(quartoLsp.session.opened_bytes / 1024).toFixed(1)} KiB)</li>
    <li>Workload: ${quartoLsp.meta.edit_count} edits; ${quartoLsp.meta.runs} fresh processes per server</li>
    <li>${quartoLsp.servers.map((server) => `${server.label}: ${server.version}; ${server.runs[0].diagnostic_mode} diagnostics`).join(". ")}</li>
  </ul>
</div>`;
```

@fig-lsp-quarto-latency shows median times from opening or editing a document to
receiving diagnostics, along with response times for document-symbol requests.
Tooltips include p95 and the number of diagnostics or symbols returned.

```{ojs}
//| label: fig-lsp-quarto-latency
//| echo: false
//| fig-cap: "Quarto LSP latency in milliseconds on a logarithmic scale. Tools
//|   appear on the x-axis; colors identify requests. Dots show medians. Tooltips
//|   include p95, sample counts, and the median number of returned diagnostics
//|   or symbols. Lower is faster."

Plot.plot({
    width,
    height: 320,
    marginLeft: 70,
    marginRight: 30,
    marginBottom: 40,
    x: { label: null, domain: quartoLsp.servers.map((s) => s.label) },
    y: {
        type: "log",
        tickFormat: d3.format(",~g"),
        ticks: timeTicks(quartoLspLatencies.map((d) => d.median)),
        label: "Request latency (ms, log scale)",
        grid: true,
    },
    color: {
        legend: true,
        label: null,
        domain: ["Open to diagnostics", "Document symbols", "Edit to diagnostics"],
        scheme: "tableau10",
    },
    marks: [
        Plot.dot(quartoLspLatencies, {
            x: "server",
            y: "median",
            fill: "metric",

                "p95 (ms)": "p95",
                samples: "samples",
                "results (median)": "results",
            },
            tip: true,
        }),
    ],
});
```

Panache has shorter median times for all three measurements in these runs. Both
servers return outlines and report no error diagnostics, though their outlines
contain different numbers of symbols.

The table below reports median initialization times and memory use across the
three sessions. Panache uses less resident memory at each measured stage.

```{ojs}
//| label: render-lsp-quarto-memory
//| echo: false

quartoLspResourceMetrics = [
    [
        "Initialize (ms)",
        (s) => (s.aggregate.timings.init_seconds * 1000).toFixed(2),
    ],
    ["Baseline RSS (MB)", (s) => s.aggregate.milestones.baseline.rss_mb],
    ["Files open RSS (MB)", (s) => s.aggregate.milestones.settled.rss_mb],
    ["After edits RSS (MB)", (s) => s.aggregate.milestones.edited.rss_mb],
    ["After edits PSS (MB)", (s) => s.aggregate.milestones.edited.pss_mb],
    ["Peak RSS (MB)", (s) => s.aggregate.milestones.peak.rss_mb],
];

html`<table class="table">
  <thead><tr><th>Metric</th>${quartoLsp.servers.map((s) => html`<th>${s.label}</th>`)}</tr></thead>
  <tbody>${quartoLspResourceMetrics.map(
        ([label, value]) =>
            html`<tr><td>${label}</td>${quartoLsp.servers.map((s) => html`<td>${value(s)}</td>`)}</tr>`,
    )}</tbody>
</table>`;
```

## Methodology {#methodology}

### Formatting and Linting

Individual-document comparisons start a fresh process for each file. Repository
comparisons process tracked files in a single invocation per tool and
repository. CLI caches are disabled. Failed repository runs have null timings in
the data and are excluded from the plots.

Yamark runs with an empty configuration and external code formatters disabled
(`--config /dev/null --skip-embedded-formatters`). Its default wrapping and
style settings apply. Yamark uses [source spans and formatting
plans](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/yamark/blob/v0.3.0/src/core/markdown.rs)
and preserves display math as opaque content. Panache builds the lossless syntax
tree also used by its linter and language server, and parses and formats TeX
math. These differences describe the work each formatter performs; the
benchmarks do not isolate their individual costs.

### Markdown Sessions {#markdown-sessions}

The runner starts three fresh processes per server in alternating order. Each
session opens the same files, obtains diagnostics using the server's advertised
pull or push mode, primes navigation requests, and waits for background work to
settle. It then times warm requests and the edit workload.

Requests run serially over stdio. Each target gets two unmeasured warmup rounds
and 20 measured rounds per session. Medians and p95 pool the measured samples
from all three sessions. Document-symbol requests cover the three largest open
files. Hover, definition, references, and rename use the reference link appended
to the largest file. References include the declaration; rename returns edits
without applying them.

The edit workload performs 1,000 fixed-width reference-label renames per
session, each followed by a definition request. Edit-to-definition timings
include all 1,000 edits, with no discarded warmups. The total edit runtime
excludes the final diagnostics and memory-settling wait. A failed or timed-out
request fails the benchmark.

The runner samples the server and its descendants through Linux `/proc` every
150 ms. Background work has settled when CPU use stays below 5% of one core for
five seconds. Workspace and open-file readiness timings end at the start of
their respective quiet periods, confirmed only after the five seconds have
elapsed. These estimates retain sampling error.

Memory measurements use the same sampler. Baseline, files-open, and after-edits
measurements follow quiet periods. Peak is the largest sampled value during the
complete session. The charts show medians across the three sessions; the JSON
retains each session's measurements.

### Quarto Sessions

The runner starts three fresh sessions per server. Each session opens the files
serially, measures document-symbol requests, and performs 100 full-document
replacements that change an appended heading in the computations guide. Full
replacements accommodate q2's synchronization mode. A final outline request must
contain the last edited heading.

File opens have no warmups. Symbol requests have two warmup rounds and 20
measured rounds per file per session. Latency medians and p95 pool samples
across all three sessions. Each edit waits for diagnostics before the next
begins. Panache uses pull diagnostics, with a request immediately after each
open or change; q2 pushes diagnostics after processing the notification. This
comparison does not measure Panache's debounced push mode.

Both servers must accept every document without error diagnostics and return a
nonempty outline. Empty diagnostic sets count as successful analyses; empty
symbol results, protocol errors, and timeouts fail the benchmark.

Initialization measures process launch through the `initialize` response. Memory
uses the same process-tree sampler and five-second quiet periods as the Markdown
comparison. q2 performs open-document parsing and outline analysis; Panache also
retains its syntax trees and analysis database.

## Reproducibility

Run these commands from the repository root:

```bash
# Measure formatting on individual documents and whole repositories.
task bench:formatter

# Measure linting on individual documents and whole repositories.
task bench:linter

# Measure both language-server comparisons, including memory use.
task bench:lsp
```

The tasks download the benchmark documents and check that the required tools are
available. The formatting and linting comparisons use `hyperfine` and `jq`. The
language-server comparisons require Linux with `/proc` and Python 3, plus
Marksman and q2 for their respective workloads. Outside the development
environment, install Yamark and record its version:

```bash
uv tool install yamark==0.3.0
export PANACHE_BENCH_YAMARK_VERSION=0.3.0
```

The scripts in [`benches/`](https://github.com/jolars/panache/tree/main/benches)
write the committed JSON files next to this document. These files supply the
charts, machine details, and tool versions shown above. Previewing or rendering
the documentation reads the saved results without running the benchmarks.

To refresh an individual comparison, run its script:

```bash
bash benches/compare_all.sh --json --out docs/guide/performance_data.json
bash benches/compare_lint_single.sh --out docs/guide/performance_lint_single_data.json
bash benches/compare_repo_suite.sh --mode format --track markdown --out docs/guide/performance_repo_markdown_format_data.json
bash benches/compare_repo_suite.sh --mode format --track quarto --out docs/guide/performance_repo_quarto_format_data.json
bash benches/compare_repo_suite.sh --mode lint --track markdown --out docs/guide/performance_repo_markdown_lint_data.json
bash benches/compare_repo_suite.sh --mode lint --track quarto --out docs/guide/performance_repo_quarto_lint_data.json
bash benches/compare_lsp_memory.sh
bash benches/compare_lsp_quarto.sh
```

The Quarto script downloads a pinned q2 release and verifies its SHA-256 hash,
or uses the executable specified by `Q2_BIN`.

After refreshing the JSON, clear this page's freeze cache and re-render it to
pick up the new results:

```bash
rm -rf docs/_freeze/guide/performance
quarto render docs/guide/performance.qmd
```
